We already know what the “Night of Destiny” is: “In that Night the angels and the Spirit descend … and there is peace until the break of dawn” (Qur'an 97:1–5). These are the verses recited over “the Imam of this age” at his birth, precisely because he is that Night. When the Ismaili interpreter discovers the same secret in the inner meaning of the Cross as in the Night of Destiny, his interpretation approaches the mystery of the Cross of Light in the Acts of John, which replaces the outward Cross of Calvary. The secret of the Night of Destiny is that it is our present cycle of concealment, lasting until the dawn of the Imam's appearance.

The mystery of this Night is one with the mystery of the Cross of Light. That is why Jesus foretold and prefigured the Paraclete, the Imam of Resurrection. The Night of Destiny transforms the night of concealment (ghaybat), just as the Cross of Light, made up of all souls of light, transforms the Cross of Calvary. In both cases, this transfiguration comes about through those who hear the same Call. Because the Night itself is the Imam, the dawn it announces is already present, for and through each faithful follower, in the “entirely new Call” to which we heard the Fifth and Sixth Imams allude a few pages ago.

The imaginative consciousness—the faculty by which spiritual realities are perceived in images—makes such visionary anticipations possible because it perceives events in the Malakut, the spiritual world. Since the soul itself is the place where these events unfold, chronological distances fall away. Shi'i consciousness can already hear the words that the Imam will one day address to humanity, because he is already speaking them in the world of the soul. And the words in which he announces himself ring out triumphantly: in the essence of his being, he gathers together the entire meaning of prophecy and walayat.

Standing against the sacred sanctuary of the Kaaba, the Imam declares that whoever wishes to dispute with him about Adam should know that he, the Imam, is closer to Adam than any other human being. He makes the same claim concerning every prophet: I am closest to Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, Muhammad. “I am closest to the Qur'an, closest to the tradition of the Prophet.” More forcefully still, he names each pair formed by a prophet and his first Imam: whoever has set his heart on Adam and Seth, Adam's son and Imam, should know that I am Adam and Seth.

And so on: I am Noah and Shem; I am Abraham and Ishmael; I am Moses and Joshua; I am Jesus and Simon; I am Muhammad and the Commander of the Faithful; I am Hasan and Husayn; I am all the Imams. Anyone who has read God's ancient books—the books of Adam, Noah, and Abraham, the Torah, the Psalms, and the Gospel—must recognize me, for they all speak of me.

Then comes the solemn appeal: “I adjure, in God's name, everyone who hears my words, now that the Witness has appeared among you—the one who until now was Hidden.” With the appearance of the one called the Resurrector (Qa'im), the era of all the sacred Laws (shari'at) reaches its completion. His coming brings back into this world the companions, the “knights,” who will fight beside him in the final struggle that must bring our aeon to its end before the Great Resurrection (Qiyamat kubra).
The pilgrims of whom it is said, “Blessed are those who leave their homeland…,” will surely answer the Imam's call.

But not everyone will do so. Here Shi'i eschatology reveals its deepest foreboding. It is as though the Resurrection cannot be announced without alarming those who have seized possession of the “divine cause” and used it to subject others to their ambitions, holding each person's destiny captive. A tradition attributed to the Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir, shows the last Imam, the Resurrector, approaching the city of Kufa. A procession of several thousand men comes out to meet him. They are all thoroughly respectable people: professional reciters of the Qur'an, doctors of religious Law, and so forth—in short, the whole company of authoritarian devotees that official piety has built into a social force. Every one of them rejects the Imam: “Son of Fatima! Go back where you came from. We have no need of you. We have no need of a son of Fatima.”

When I first read this text, I had the sense that I had encountered something like these words before, sounding from far away. They led me back to the refusal spoken by the Grand Inquisitor in Dostoevsky's famous novel, addressing Christ, returned to Seville, on the night the Inquisitor holds him prisoner: “Why have You come back to disturb us? … Have You the right to reveal to us a single one of the mysteries of the world from which You come? … Had You forgotten that tranquillity, and even death, are preferable to man than the freedom to distinguish good from evil? … Go away and do not come back, ever again.”

The resemblance between the reception awaiting the returning Imam and that awaiting the returning Christ was striking. I mentioned it to a shaykh whom I knew to be both profound and discreet. In reply, he first reminded me of texts saying that the Twelfth Imam passes through a concealment comparable to Joseph's after his brothers sold him, and that of all human beings he most closely resembles Christ, for he must return just as Christ will return. The Qur'an (4:156) teaches that Christ did not die upon the Cross but was “taken up by God,” as Enoch and Elijah had been. When the Imam returns, the doctors of religious Law, in Kufa and elsewhere, will tell him in vain: “Go away and never come back.”

For the Imam will wield a sword not forged from earthly metal, a sword that penetrates souls. With him will come not only the mighty, proud Companions sleeping their mysterious sleep until his arrival, but legions of angels: those who were with Noah in the ark; with Abraham when he was cast into the fire; with Moses when he divided the sea; with Jesus when God took him up; with Muhammad at the Battle of Badr; and with Imam Husayn on the day of his martyrdom at Karbala, although Husayn refused even their help. Then Christ, the Messiah (Masih), will return. A magnificent visionary ceremony shows him descending at dawn from the white minaret east of Damascus, supported by two angels, and performing the Prayer behind the Imam. “Yes,” the shaykh told me, “Christ son of Mary will return.

“But you see, he will not return until our Imam has destroyed the power of all those who might still say to him: ‘Go away and never come back.’” Any commentary would only weaken the force of that remark. The shaykh had meditated on the relationship between Christianity and Shi'ism, between Christ and the Imam, in a way that was his own secret. Yet this secret shines through the many references to Christ found in Shi'i teaching about the Imams.

Consider the extraordinary sermons in which, speaking through the lips of one Imam or another, an eternal Imam declares: “I am the one called Elijah in the Gospel”—making Shi'ism a witness to the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor. Or again: “I am the Christ who heals the blind and the lepers, who gives life to birds made of clay and disperses the clouds”—“that is, the second Christ,” a commentary specifies. “I am he and he is I (ana huwa wa huwa ana).” There is also a direct retelling of an episode in the Infancy Gospels, the teaching of the secrets of the philosophical alphabet, in which the young Imam Muhammad al-Baqir, the Fifth Imam, simply takes Jesus' place.

And there is the wonderful visionary dream of Princess Nargis, mother of the Twelfth Imam, in which she sees Christ and his apostles, the Prophet and his Imams, ascending the same pulpit of light together—a story we translated earlier. We may add that four of the Gospel Beatitudes appear in the spiritual testament of the Seventh Imam of Twelver Shi'ism, Imam Musa Kazim (d. 183/799). For a long time these texts, these events, and the considerable writings they inspired remained unknown in the West. Once brought to light, however, they confront scholars of sacred learning, and everyone concerned with comparative theology among the “religions of the Book,” with questions too new to be settled by ready-made answers.

Perhaps we can avoid such ready-made answers, while taking inspiration from what I earlier called the “mystery of Pentecost,” by making one final comparison. Its implications remain to be explored, but by now the reader may already have thought of it. I have in mind Joachim of Fiore and his followers in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Shi'i spiritual philosophers speak of the “eternal religion” and the “Paraclete.” Drawing upon a tradition of prophetic Christianity, Joachim's followers speak of the “Eternal Gospel” and the “reign of the Paraclete.”

For Shi'is, the coming of the Imam-Paraclete will inaugurate the reign of the pure spiritual meaning of divine revelations. This is what they mean by the “Eternal Religion,” and it is what the reformed Ismailism of Alamut sought, perhaps prematurely, to bring about through the proclamation of the Great Resurrection on 8 August 1164. For Joachim's followers, the reign of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, will be the age in which spiritual understanding (intelligentia spiritualis) of the Scriptures prevails. This is what they mean by the “Eternal Gospel.” The resonance between the two is striking.

We can speak of a shared “hermeneutic situation”—a common way of understanding—despite the differences arising from the Qur'anic Revelation. Those very differences make the comparison all the more instructive.

The driving idea behind the Eternal Gospel in the teaching of Joachim of Fiore (1145–1202), the celebrated founder of the Ordo Florensis (Saint John in Flower), is that humanity develops through the unceasing work of the Holy Spirit. This development will culminate in the reign of the Paraclete promised in John's Gospel. At its culmination, human beings will attain the Spirit's perfect freedom, born of the love that the Holy Spirit awakens in the human heart. Adam will no longer be under the satanic power that prompts him to choose “against God.” It is true that Joachim's teaching influenced thinkers century after century, reaching even the philosophy of freedom in German idealism.

Yet we must avoid a fundamental confusion. The unfolding of the “history of salvation” is not the unfolding of a principle inherent in history, advancing in a straight line according to what is now called “historical causation.” Quite the contrary: salvation unfolds only through the Holy Spirit's continuous and active intervention. This creative intervention repeatedly breaks the course imposed on things by bodily desire and worldly ambition. It is not a natural transition in which the old disappears to make room for the new.

Each time, it is an act of spiritual creation. Such creations are continually threatened by the world. Their gravest danger is that the very idea of creation by the Spirit may be degraded into the idea of an ordinary historical power at work within the world. That is precisely how sacred history—the history that takes place, as we would say, in the Malakut—is turned into secular history, how an inward history is replaced by an outward, supposedly objective one. This is the process of secularization in its specifically metaphysical sense: the elimination of metaphysics itself.
Yet such a process cannot accommodate the idea of the Holy Spirit working in human hearts, any more than it can accommodate the Imam-Paraclete working in the hearts of his followers.
For Joachim, this work of the Spirit unfolds within the famous scheme dividing the history of salvation into three ages, each bearing the Seal of one Person of the divine Trinity.

First, there is the age of the Father, the revelation of the Law. Here human sinfulness comes to the fore, although the ideal of the coming spiritual life (vita spiritualis) is already foreshadowed in figures such as the prophet Elijah and John the Baptist.

Second comes the age of the Son, the revelation of Redemption. Humanity becomes the “Son of God” and discovers deliverance from sin. Its representative spiritual figure is the cleric, or better still the monk, as conceived in the ideal of the Byzantine Greek Church.
Third comes the age of the Spirit, marked by the arrival of the order of the viri spirituales, the spiritual human beings in whom the divine character of humanity's creative nature is revealed.

Each age has its own kind of human being and its own spiritual way of life. The viri spirituales of the age of the Spirit are neither “fathers,” as defined by the Old Testament, nor “sons,” as defined by the New. They are angelic spirits, formed in the image and likeness of the Holy Spirit (Angelici spiritus, qui neque patres sunt, neque filii, ad similitudinem Spiritus Sancti). To the world around them they can appear only as something beyond the ordinary human. Their knowledge is essentially spiritual, with nothing in common with the doctrina litteralis, the learning tied to the literal text, of the clerical Church. That Church now occupies the position of the merchants driven from the Temple.

If the Father's age can be represented by manual labour, and the Son's by the efforts of doctrinal theology, the Spirit's age is an outpouring of hymns, an intoxication of the spirit (ebrietas), best expressed by jubilatio and gaudium: exultation and joy. This is the very “joy” which, in Shi'i language, names the appearance of the Imam-Paraclete, when, as we have been told, trees and stones will speak. One might say that the difference between the viri spirituales and the clerics is the same as that between the urafa, the mystics and spiritual philosophers, and the fuqaha, the doctors of religious Law who reject the Imam when he appears.

The viri spirituales, in whom the contemplative life (vita contemplativa) reaches its highest form, are the people of Joachim's Ecclesia spiritualis, the Spiritual Church. It is “virginal” because it “knows no man”: it has no part in the interests and ambitions of those who are not spiritual human beings. (Here we may recall the Shi'i injunction to befriend everything that draws one nearer to the Imam, and to keep apart from whatever is not the Imam, is not directed toward him, or is directed against him. We have seen this as the “fourth pillar” of the Shaykhi school, supporting both the idea of a hidden spiritual hierarchy and the idea of the final transformation.)

This Ecclesia spiritualis, this reign of the Paraclete, is the “Church of John” succeeding the “Church of Peter.” As Berdyaev writes, the Church of John is not a guardian of the poor adjusted to the weakness of sinners, to the mediocrity of humanity at large, or even indulgent toward every form of human wretchedness. It is the eternal, mysterious Church, “discovering within itself the true face of man and of his ecstasy upon the heights.” The idea of the Paraclete's reign as the final form of spiritual life could only strike at and shake the central pillar of Peter's Church, the institutional Roman Church.

In this vision that institution becomes merely a transitional stage in the history of salvation. The papacy belongs to the second age, that of the Son; it disappears with the Paraclete's reign, when the viri spirituales, the people of the Spirit, succeed the bishops. It would be illuminating to compare the way Joachim's spiritual interpretation of the four Gospels works toward the coming of the Paraclete with the way Shi'i interpretation of the Qur'an works toward the coming of the Imam.

The passage from one age to another is not the result of a historical cause operating within the world. Each transition is a resurrection. Only a creative act of the Holy Spirit can set an age condemned to die upon the path toward resurrection from the dead. This is also the technical sense of qiyamat, resurrection, in Ismaili spiritual philosophy. Without that ever-renewed act of creation, every tradition merely lengthens its funeral procession along the road of historical causation. No Tradition remains alive without continual rebirth: an ever-new birth.

The ages of the Father and the Son lead toward the age of the Spirit, the reign of the Paraclete, just as the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of walayat lead toward the final Seal of walayat: the Twelfth Imam, in whom our thinkers have recognized the Paraclete. The Church of John, the Paraclete's reign, is the Nova Hierosolyma, the New Jerusalem, built of different stones after a migration that transforms the meaning of the departure from Egypt, the land of exile. We have heard the call to this migration in Shi'ism too, in the Imam's words: “Tuba li'l-ghuraba!

“Blessed are those who leave their homeland for the sake of the Spirit.” And we have been told that humanity continues to exist thanks to these travellers, who, unknown to the multitude, perform the divine service of the highest “heavenly” chivalry. Through that service—through their union with the Intelligence that is the Holy Spirit—the higher worlds remain in communication with ours. We might therefore compare the viri spirituales with the “Friends of God,” since both belong to the same “spiritual chivalry.”

The reign of the Paraclete is the manifestation of these spiritual human beings, these Friends of God, into whom the Holy Spirit pours intelligentia spiritualis in the new Temple. Their knowledge is no longer a literal understanding shut up within itself, something that can be fixed in the written letter, whether of theology or of the most modern science. It is an inexhaustible treasure of wisdom, a spring of living water welling up into eternal life (fons aquae salientis in vitam aeternam). And here, once again, as so often in our texts, we return to the threshold of the “Spring of Life” (ayn al-hayat).

Yet does this “vision of ecstasy upon the heights” contain its own danger—a temptation to rush ahead? We can glimpse the danger in the very success of Joachim's idea: not only in its later development among the Hussites of fifteenth-century Bohemia, but also in its powerful influence upon so many philosophers and theologians of history—philosophers such as Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel, and spiritual thinkers such as Franz von Baader, Solovyov, Berdyaev, and Merezhkovsky. Philosophers, admittedly, bear a responsibility here from which those who are “theosophers,” in the original sense of the word, are exempt.

A few pages ago, I warned against the danger that the Paraclete idea in Joachim's teaching might be secularized. That danger became reality. Philosophy treated it as a triumph to separate the idea of the Paraclete from the spiritual world that both grounds it and guarantees its truth. Agnosticism turned the Church of John into a social messianism, a caricature of the original. Despair methodically closed off every way by which human beings might escape the absurdity of death. A phenomenology of the historical Spirit was no longer a spiritual interpretation guided by the Holy Spirit. And perhaps the primary cause of this change was a confusion of places and times.

The realm in which sacred history, the history of salvation, takes place is not the realm addressed by the philosophy of history. The Holy Spirit's creative action breaks through both history and the philosophy of history, for it sets human beings free from them. It takes place in the invisible spiritual world, the Malakut. Nor does it take place in the chronological time of outward history. Joachim of Fiore's three ages are not three successive periods of historical time. In fact, we know no exact dates separating them. If we tried to identify such boundaries, it would be difficult to find in the events of outward history the evidence needed to draw them.

Rather, the three ages are units of existential time, of inward time. Think here of Semnani's psycho-spiritual time (zaman anfusi), of subtle time (zaman latif), and of the measure of time allotted to each being in the thought of Qazi Sa'id Qummi. The succession of these ages is played out within souls, in the mystery of each individual soul: in its consent and refusal, its generosity and its withholding, or, in Qazi Sa'id's terms, in the states through which its own eternally allotted measure of time passes. In historical time, the ages actually coexist.

It is not within humanity's collective historical time that the Church of John succeeds the Church of Peter. Such a succession can occur only by bringing historical time itself to an end, together with its chains of events and determining precedents. How could we place it within history, when history is no longer there—just as concealment (ghaybat) “is no longer there” when the Imam appears? Existential time breaks the fabric of historical time for every soul that enters the world of the Spirit and anticipates the mystery of death.

But outward history continues after each soul's breakthrough. Each soul must break through it in turn. Thus the two Churches are divided among souls: invisibly, within each soul, the Church of John succeeds the Church of Peter, in the measure of time belonging to that soul alone, a measure that is also the measure of its being.

Yet because souls coexist in this world's mode of existence, the two Churches also coexist in historical time. This is already the arresting meaning that Joachim drew from a single Gospel passage, where Jesus says to Peter, “Feed my sheep,” only to say immediately afterward, speaking of John, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?” (John 21:16 ff., 22).

Does the fate of Joachim's idea in the West not give us two reasons for reflection? On the one hand, it supports the comparison we have just made between the Ecclesia spiritualis of the Paraclete's reign and the coming of the Imam, whom his followers recognize as the Paraclete promised in John's Gospel. On the other, it reveals a difference that, if properly understood, may open an unexplored perspective for philosophical thought. We have already noticed that familiar words in our languages, such as secularization and laicization, have no exact equivalents in Arabic or Persian. These terms presuppose the existence of clerics, and thus a clergy, clerical status, and finally the phenomenon of the Church.

But that phenomenon is absent in Islam. And in Joachim's view, the Church of the clergy is precisely what characterizes the age of the Son. Islam and Islamic spirituality, however, have no age of the Son. In Shi'i theology, the teaching about the Imams corresponds to Christology in Christian theology.

But everything we have seen shows that it corresponds no less to a theology of the Holy Spirit as Paraclete. This double correspondence is also found in certain early Christologies, where the distinction between the Son and the Spirit had not yet been clearly established. Its implications reach very far, and we cannot pursue all of them here.

For Islamic spiritual philosophy, sacred history moves not through three stages but through two: descent (nuzul) and ascent (su'ud); origin (mabda') and return (ma'ad); the revelation of the sacred text (tanzil) and its spiritual interpretation (ta'wil); and so on. It cannot have a reign of the “Son,” precisely because the Qur'anic Revelation comes after Christianity, after the reign and history of the “Son.” It passes directly from the cycle of prophecy, the reign of the Law (shari'at) revealed through the prophets, to the cycle of walayat, of intelligentia spiritualis: the cycle of the Imamate, whose Seal is the Twelfth Imam. Here there is no reason to say that the reign of the creative Spirit presupposes “redemption”: it is that redemption.

There is thus no need for an intervening age like the one in which the specifically Christian process of secularization arises. That process follows from the Church of the clergy, and it in turn explains why the political and social ideologies of the West are secularized theologies. Philosophy may no longer be the “handmaid of theology” (ancilla theologiae), but it has become the handmaid of sociology. The importation into Islam of a secularization and an ideology alien to its theological history could therefore be all the more disastrous.

By contrast, our Shi'i thinkers' identification of the Imam with the Paraclete promises a particularly liberating meaning. It agrees perfectly with their identification of the Active Intelligence with the Holy Spirit: an identification that puts each philosopher in direct contact with the spiritual world, without the intervention of any teaching authority, clerical or secular. Where no clerical authority of this kind has existed, it cannot turn into its opposite—something like a post-Church.

But wherever secularization and the reshaping of religion as a social institution presuppose the Church, and hence the age of the “Son,” they show by that very fact that the passage from the Church of the clerics to the Church of John, the Church of the viri spirituales, has been missed. There may still be a “philosophy of Spirit,” but the Spirit itself will soon have vanished from it. Islamic spiritual philosophy, like Christian spiritual philosophy, will instead continue to pursue a metaphysics of the Holy Spirit. In inward sacred history, the cycle of walayat has succeeded the prophets' cycle of shari'at.

Yet the two coexist in historical time, just as the Churches of Peter and John coexist, because the reign of the shari'at continues until the Imam-Paraclete appears. The arif, the mystic possessed of inward knowledge, is a pilgrim on the road, a salik, a homo viator. He already belongs to the reign of the Paraclete; in this sense he, too, is a follower of John.

Shall we ask how the pilgrimage to which he sacrifices everything can be reconciled with the demands of the surrounding world, the demands supposedly made by “his times”? It will always be too soon to ask that question as long as the world cannot see the Imam where he is. Because it has failed to see him where he is, the hope and preparation for the resurrection of the dead have collapsed under their own weight. Instead of the resurrection of the dead, people now expect nothing more than social revolution. But Islam is not responsible for that transformation.

It is all too easy to put Christianity on trial from the outside. Very few Christian thinkers have had the clarity and courage to confront Christianity's tragedy. Berdyaev was one of them. It is no accident that we cited him at the beginning of our inquiry and return to him now at its close. The themes he brings to light are precisely those that Shi'i spiritual philosophy and its teaching about the Imams can suggest to a student of sacred learning.

We are not trying to argue a case before the court of history; that would be as pointless as it would be absurd. We are trying to find a way toward the world—or worlds—without whose presence human beings cannot endure. Berdyaev wrote that Christianity's tragedy lay in its failure to discover the whole of the “Christology of man”: the mystery of humanity's divine nature, although discovering that mystery is the very mission of religious consciousness. “The Church of Golgotha, in which the Christological truth is only imperfectly disclosed, stands opposed to the integral Church of Christ.”

Only the discipline demanded by a free act of creation brings humanity face to face with this new aspect of Christology. In a passage inspired throughout by the spirit of John and Joachim, Berdyaev writes: “If redemption demands great obedience, creation—the creative act—demands great daring. We glimpse Christ advancing only when we make a bold attempt. The spirit of obedience has always seen in Christ only the Crucified, only the aspect of the redeemer. The sacrifice of courage, the heroic decision, is needed to launch ourselves beyond these safe shores.

“We must stand without fear over the abyss. The third revelation in Spirit will have no sacred text; it will not be a voice from above. It will take place within man and humanity. It will be the anthropological revelation, the discovery of the Christology of man.”

Our Shi'i spiritual philosophers know, too, that the awaited Imam, the Paraclete, will bring no new shari'at, no new sacred Book, but will reveal the meaning hidden in all the sacred texts. And he himself is that meaning, as the Perfect Human (Insan kamil, anthropos teleios). When the Russian philosopher meditates on the significance of the future Christ's appearance, and when our Iranian Shi'i thinkers meditate on the coming of the “Awaited Imam,” both are awaiting the same full “anthropological revelation”—the disclosure of what humanity truly is. This revelation cannot come from outside. It must take place within human beings living in the Spirit. For this is not a revelation humanity is still waiting to receive from God. It is one that God is waiting to receive from humanity.

But only a metaphysics of the last things—an eschatological metaphysics—can give us a horizon wide enough for such a thought. That is why our texts have led us to consider Joachim's understanding of the final age. A tradition offered us the image of the “Hidden Treasure,” longing, in its solitude before the worlds, to be known. Ismaili spiritual philosophers derive the name of God, Allah, from the root w-l-h, with its suggestion of grief and longing. Berdyaev, for his part, wrote that the image of “God's sorrow over man and love for man brings us close to the ultimate secrets.” The mystics have spoken of the birth of God within the human being, he says.

But there is another mystery: the birth of the human being within God. Humanity cries out for God to be born within it; God cries out for humanity to be born within him. We earlier encountered a verse from Isaiah translated by a Kabbalist: “And in all their anguish, it was He who was anguished.” The Russian philosopher called this birth of humanity within God the “Christological consciousness of man,” the “new aeon,” the “reign of the Paraclete.”

What, then, of everything that has appeared, and continues to appear, in Shi'i consciousness under the figure of the Twelfth Imam? What of the events of his sacred story—his birth, concealment, appearances, and coming as Paraclete? Even, and especially, if these are visionary events rather than historical events in the ordinary sense—even, and especially, if the story teaches us less about what happened outwardly than about what appeared and was genuinely experienced within Shi'i consciousness—all of it must now acquire meaning for a Western reader. From now on, no attempt we make at an eschatological metaphysics ought to ignore the Shi'i theme of the Hidden Imam.

The Shi'i spiritual philosopher Haydar Amoli showed us Adam—humanity—bowed beneath the “burden that the heavens, the earth, and the mountains had refused,” but that Adam had agreed to bear. This burden was what Haydar Amoli technically calls ontological tawhid: the inwardly lived recognition that the One alone truly is, the hidden meaning of the monotheistic profession of faith. If humanity is too weak to bear that meaning, then in losing God it loses itself. All that remains is to cry, “God is dead,” without realizing that this is the cry of someone already dead: humanity itself died first. Unfortunately, our fashionable theologies and philosophies of the death of God and the death of humanity are still the scholastic exercises of more or less secularized clerics.

The inward meaning of tawhid, culminating in the highest of all the divine manifestations that mark humanity's spiritual growth, is the mystery of the supreme theophany: the appearance of the last Imam, finally bathing in peace and light those ravaged and devastated Earths “of which there are as many as there are human hearts,” as Haydar Amoli said. With the coming of the Seal of walayat, the teaching about the Imams reaches its fulfilment and brings forth the dawn of humanity's resurrection—the day of humanity's birth within God. Here, too, we may say that “the ultimate secret lies in this: the divine mystery and the human mystery are one and the same mystery; within God is kept the mystery of humanity, and within humanity the secret of God.”

This brings us, at last, to the innermost life of the Shi'i spiritual seeker: to what the theme of the Twelfth Imam means in lived experience. His invisible Presence safeguards the spiritual life against being reduced to a social phenomenon. It is a Presence at once infinitely distant and intimately near: withdrawn to the outermost limit of our aeon, yet immediately present in the depths of the heart. It is tied to no fixed geographical place, yet it can break into any place and carry the person to whom the Imam appears into the Imam's own world: to the Green Island, for example, or to some uncharted place in the heart of the desert, beyond the reach of any map. We have seen examples of this. The Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, is above all the form in which the invisible Personal Guide makes himself known to Shi'i consciousness.

The theme is inexhaustibly rich, and it defines a kind of spiritual life as intensely personal as Shi'i spirituality itself. We have encountered many variations on it. There are the Uwaysis, those who are set upon the spiritual Path by an invisible Guide, without needing any human master.

There is the “Perfect Nature,” the philosopher's personal angel among the Ishraqiyun, the philosophers of illumination who inherited the Hermetic tradition; the “heavenly companion” of the Gnostics; Mani's “heavenly Twin”; the “invisible master” (ostad ghaybi), the “witness in heaven,” spoken of by Najm al-Din Kubra and his school. (Who is the seeker, and who is the one sought? Kubra answers: “The one sought is the divine Light; the seeker is a particle of that Light.” He perceives the presence of the “invisible Personal Guide” in the meeting blaze of two flames, one reaching from heaven and the other from earth.) There are the “prophets of your being” in Semnani; “the angel who speaks within you” among certain Kabbalists; the “Friend of God” for Rulman Merswin, and others.

All are recurring forms of a single archetypal Figure. In Shi'i spirituality, this figure reaches its highest and most commanding manifestation in the Imam, the “Friend of God,” as invisible Personal Guide. Between him and the faithful person he guides there is formed a bond of knightly loyalty, expressed most movingly in the “pilgrim's prayer” that we shall translate on the final page. This bond springs from the feeling of the traveller, the salik, the homo viator. He is not a sinner or an invalid but an exile, someone far from home, searching for the road that will take him “home” again. The Imam shows him that road. And the person to whom the Imam reveals it through his intimate presence has no need of a human master or guide.

One of the best-known Uwaysis was the Iranian Sufi Abu'l-Hasan Kharraqani (d. 425/1034), to whom the following saying is attributed: “I am astonished at disciples who declare that they must have this or that master. You know perfectly well that I have never been taught by any human being. God himself was my guide, although I have the greatest respect for all masters.” Kharraqani was guided by the spiritual presence, the “Angel” (ruhaniyya), of Abu Yazid Bastami; Attar of Nishapur (d. around 617/1220) had for his guide the Angel, or “being of light,” of Hallaj. We could assemble many testimonies of this kind.

I shall recall only one already discussed here, showing that such teaching is still given today. An eminent shaykh, a professor at the theological university of Qom, advised his students to study mystical spiritual philosophy and practise Sufi spirituality, but to avoid entering a tariqa, a Sufi order. To join an order is to bind oneself in subjection to a shaykh, and thereby to confine oneself within that shaykh's personality and spiritual horizon. The Shi'i mystic, the irfani, must choose the Imam himself directly as his qutb, his spiritual pole, and follow this Personal Guide without an intermediary. His only shaykh is the Imam.

All spiritual teaching thus centres on the quest for and encounter with the Personal Guide. Its purpose is to awaken, in the depths of a person, the capacity to meet the “invisible personal master” who is the Imam.

Indeed, the word imam itself means guide. This personal encounter gives Shi'i spirituality its most distinctive form. We saw an exemplary instance in the life of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsai. That is why, in Book I, chapter VII, we dwelt at length on the mutual relationship between knowing—or becoming conscious of—the Imam and knowing—or becoming conscious of—oneself. Through the particular calling that Shi'i teaching about the Imams addresses to every spiritual seeker, prophetic religion reaches its fulfilment. The Imam, the Guide, brings no new Law. He uncovers and resolves the hidden meaning of all prophetic revelations, enabling his followers to be born into the reign of the Paraclete.

Any reader familiar with the changes sweeping through the modern East will inevitably ask: what will these things mean to the generations to come? What, for example, does the mysterious figure of the Twelfth Imam mean to the Iranian young people of our day? I think the reflections that have emerged throughout this long inquiry show that I am not inclined to minimize the immensely serious problems raised by the transformations now under way.

But I have considered these problems according to measures that do not necessarily coincide with those of today's prevailing anthropology. For that very reason, I am all the more struck by certain enduring features of spiritual life that escape, and always will escape, every survey, sociological or otherwise. Each Shi'i has always maintained absolute discretion on these matters—the practice of taqiyya. This is why I attach such importance to a testimony I related elsewhere and now think it fitting to reproduce.

It came from a young Iranian friend of mine, not yet thirty, highly representative of students educated in the West, among whom practically all the conditions for spiritual uprooting are present. (We might say: all the conditions that lead the young Parthian prince in the “Hymn of the Pearl,” in the Acts of Thomas, to forget his origins.) He was completing his studies at a Swiss university. That country might have offered him everything he could wish for; yet he spent most of his evenings with another young Iranian student, nostalgically recalling the wide deserts of Iran and the pilgrimage to the holy city of Qom, about 140 kilometres south of Tehran.

Then one night he made, in a dream, the pilgrimage he had longed to undertake in waking life. His account bore so clearly the marks of an initiatory dream, and the power of the archetype was so strongly felt in it, that I asked him to write it down. With his permission, and referring to him discreetly by his initials, H. B., I reproduce his account here.

“One night I dreamed that my friend and I had set out on foot from Tehran for Qom. We were not wearing our everyday clothes but the garments worn by dervishes, the Sufis, in our country. We followed paths through the fields leading south toward Qom. We were about to enter the desert south of Tehran when immense creatures suddenly appeared before us, something like dragons. All at once I could no longer see my friend. I had the impression that he had turned back and gone north. I felt that I was alone.

“But now I found something like a spear in my hands, so long that I had never seen anything like it in real life. I fought the dragons for a long, long time. At last I must have succeeded in cutting them to pieces, for I saw that a torrent flowing nearby was carrying away their dismembered bodies, and I myself was immersed in the torrent. I came out of that bath and felt that I was naked. Then someone threw a long piece of cloth across my shoulders.

“At that moment the ground beneath me seemed to be giving off steam or mist, so that nothing could be seen. Suddenly the holy city appeared in the distance, with the glittering golden dome and minarets of its sacred precinct. I made my way toward the city and reached a crossroads covered by a vaulted roof. There someone pointed out to me the house of the Awaited Imam. Its door stood wide open. Only a short distance, a few hundred paces, separated me from the Imam's house. … At that moment I awoke from my dream.

“But it has left a deep impression on me. What matters most to me is the distance that separated me from the open door of the Imam's house. Ever since that night, I have felt that my life, whether I am dreaming or awake, consists of crossing that distance. It is the exact measure of my life. It governs the time and harmony of my whole existence. It is the real time and space that I experience upon this Earth.”

Once again, many other testimonies of this kind could be cited. All bear witness to the presence of the Hidden Imam, “invisible to the senses, but present in the hearts of his faithful,” and therefore visible in dreams or visionary encounters. The “history” of the Twelfth Imam thus continues through events kept secret within the consciousness of those devoted to him. The testimony I have been allowed to reproduce seems to gather them all into itself. Here, in modern Iran, a young Iranian of our own time teaches every student of religion what the religion of the Personal Guide means.

A religion reveals its secret most fully in its prayers and liturgies, far better than in any systematic account of its doctrines. It therefore seems fitting to close our inquiry with a prayer addressed by pilgrims to the mysterious person of the Twelfth Imam. In him, through the dream of his mother, Princess Nargis, the spiritual descendants of Christ and of Muhammad meet. Whatever a Shi'i's personal position, whether Sufi or not, the same hope stirs in all of them. As soon as they try to state it in words and explain it in one way or another, their interpretations may differ.

Yet some forms of expression stand above the rest, capable of uniting them all; these are found in the prayers addressed to the Twelfth Imam. We should recall that the Imam's very “absence”—the fact that he is not physically present to lead the communal Prayer in the mosque—has especially encouraged Shi'ism to develop forms of private devotion and liturgy. The oldest of these were taught by the Imams themselves.

Enriched over the centuries, they constitute an extensive body of literature arranged according to an exceptionally rich liturgical calendar. It deserves systematic and comparative study. (We have quoted some examples earlier.) Among these personal devotions are the “prayers of Visitation,” recited either during pilgrimage to the shrines of the holy Imams or, more simply and more often, during a “visitation in the mind,” undertaken in the quiet concentration of a private place of prayer.

We have already sketched the story of the founding of the sanctuary at Jamkaran. In Samarra, where the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam led us earlier, two shrines still stand. One houses four tombs: that of the Tenth Imam, Ali Naqi; that of his son, Imam Hasan al-Askari; that of Hasan's wife, the Byzantine princess Nargis; and that of his aunt, the venerable Hakima Khatun, sister of Imam Ali Naqi. A second shrine shelters the underground place through which the young Imam, Princess Nargis's child, Muhammad al-Qa'im or al-Mahdi, disappeared, becoming the Hidden Imam. Pious and learned Shi'is have composed many prayers for these pilgrimages, whether they are undertaken bodily or spiritually. Such texts disclose more clearly than almost anything else the deepest spirit of Shi'ism.
We have come to know that spirit as, above all, a spiritual chivalry. The pact of loyalty uniting the javanmard, the spiritual knight, to his Imam inspires ardent words and commitments.

We must understand that the passage into the reign of the Paraclete, whether in the inward time of each human being or at the close of the entire span of historical humanity, does not take place without a struggle against all the powers of denial, hardening, and death. The Shi'i mystic, too, is attentive to the impermanence of things, the passing nature of every substance, and the threat that personal existence may dissolve.

But it is one thing to accept all this as the normal law of existence, and to make the emptying away of being the aim of meditation and spiritual discipline, so as to recover the primordial Void. It is quite another to experience it as a wound in being, the result of a satanic and destructive hold that must be fought so that existence may be restored to its wholeness.

In the latter view, the governing idea is apokatastasis: the “restoration” or “return” of all things to their original purity and fullness. It was this idea that set Zoroastrian consciousness against the powers of Ahriman, and it is this idea that we find again in the Shi'i spiritual ethos. Haydar Amoli identified the Twelfth Imam with the Paraclete of the Gospel; Qutb al-Din Ashkevari identified him with the last of Zoroastrianism's three Saoshyants, the future saviours. The millennium of the last Saoshyant and the millennium of the last Imam are the setting for this struggle. Every javanmard, every knight of faith, longs to take part in it at his Imam's side.

Here, then, is the pilgrim's prayer. Like all prayers of this kind, it has the virtue of allowing both the believer of simple heart and the most deeply initiated interpreter to make its words their own, while understanding them each in their own way. I translate it here, with only some slight abridgment.

“Peace be upon you, O representative of God and successor to your rightly guided fathers, the Mahdis. Peace be upon you, heir of the spiritual heirs (awsiya) of ages past […], Scion of the Immaculate Family, Treasury of prophetic knowledge, Threshold of God that none can reach without crossing it, Path of God that none can leave without going astray. You who behold the Tree of Tuba and the Lotus Tree at the furthest boundary […], God's Guarantor to those in heaven and those on earth: peace be upon you from those who recognize you as God has made you known to them, and who give you some of the titles you deserve, although you are beyond them.

“I bear witness that you are God's Guarantor to those who lived before and those yet to come; that those who triumph are your followers, and those who are deprived are those who reject you. You preserve all knowledge and open all that was sealed […]. O my lord! I have chosen you as my Imam and Guide, my protector and teacher, and I desire no one in your place.
“I bear witness that you are the unchanging truth, in which there is no alteration; that God's promise concerning you is certain.

“However long your concealment (ghaybat) may last, however far off the appointed hour, I have no doubt. I will not join those who, knowing nothing of you, wander astray and speak foolishly of you. I remain in expectation of your Day, for you are the Intercessor whose right none may dispute, the Friend whom none may disown […].

“I call God to witness! I call his angels to witness! I call upon you yourself to witness my vow: inwardly it is what it is outwardly; in the secret of my consciousness it is exactly what my tongue declares. Be witness, then, to my promise to you, to the covenant of loyalty between you and me […] as the Lord of the worlds commands me.

“Though time stretch on, though the years of my life follow one upon another, my certainty concerning you will only grow, my love for you only deepen, and my trust in you only increase. I shall await your coming all the more eagerly, and make myself ever readier for the struggle to be fought beside you. For my own self, my possessions, my family, all that my God has granted me in this world, I give to you to dispose of as you will, O my Imam!
“If my life lasts long enough for me to see your radiant Day arise and your banners shine, here I am, your faithful follower. May I be granted the supreme Witnessing at your side!

“But if death overtakes me before you have appeared, then I ask for your intercession, yours and that of your fathers, the Immaculate Imams, so that God may count me among those whom he will allow to return (raj'at) at the hour of your coming, when your Day dawns. May my devotion to you thus bring me to the fulfilment of my longing.”

Whatever region of the Malakut may be the scene of the final struggle, whatever immaterial weapons may determine its outcome, this prayer expresses the spirit of all Iranian chivalry, from the heroes of the Zoroastrian epic to those of Shi'i Persia's mystical epic. Shi'i and Zoroastrian ideas alike become living realities in a fellowship of knights of faith. The Iranian spirit preserves and joins the ancient tradition of the pahlavan, the heroic champion, with the Abrahamic tradition of futuwwat, spiritual chivalry. The companions of the Saoshyant and the companions of the Hidden Imam alike are drawn toward the same final goal.

“May we be among those who bring about the Transfiguration of the world,” repeated a liturgical refrain of the Zoroastrian faithful. “May God hasten the joy of his coming,” says every faithful Shi'i whenever the Twelfth Imam's name is mentioned. The two brief invocations sound in unison. They bear witness to the ethic of the knight of faith, inseparable from a metaphysics of the last things: a fundamental note sounding again and again through all the complex themes of spiritual philosophy we have studied in this inquiry.

The mystic concerned with inward realities can read the pilgrim's prayer in the light of all that has been said here about the reciprocal relationship between knowledge of the Imam and knowledge of oneself. It becomes the prayer and vow of the “knight of the soul,” making a pilgrimage in quest of his own We. Not a word need be changed; the tone remains the same.

And perhaps this best gathers together what the philosopher has learned from the hospitality offered him in Iranian Islam. But there can be no spiritual hospitality without reciprocity: the guest who is welcomed must inwardly be a host who welcomes in turn. Without that reciprocity, there is no hope of understanding.
